A series of field studies conducted in the montane regions of western North America provides detailed life-history data for the Violet-green swallow (Tachycineta thalassina). During the incubation period, eggs are maintained at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime that supports the development of the altricial nestling. The age at hatching under these conditions is 14 days [ab = 14 days], a relatively short incubation period typical of small-bodied hirundines at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Newly emerged chicks are notably small, with a wet weight at birth of 1.66 grams [Wwb = 1.66 grams], a mass that underscores their extreme altriciality and total dependence on parental provisioning. This modest neonatal mass is followed by a period of exceptionally rapid somatic growth, culminating in an asymptotic nestling mass of 20.6 grams [Wwi = 20.6 grams], which is slightly less than the average adult mass of the species, reflecting the energetic constraints of reaching physical independence.

The timing of key developmental milestones in Tachycineta thalassina has been documented under the active metabolic conditions typical of the breeding season, which average around 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the time since birth at fledging for successfully reared chicks is 26 days [tx = 26 days], a duration that permits full flight feather maturation and the achievement of sustained aerial locomotion. at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]This fledging period aligns reasonably well with anecdotal reports suggesting a range of 24 to 28 days, though it lies at the upper end of the 21 to 25 day interval cited in some field guides. Following nest departure, the fledgling enters a post-fledging dispersal phase during which it continues to receive occasional provisioning from the adults. This extended parental care gradually diminishes as the juvenile bird refines its foraging skills, ultimately preparing it for the energetic demands of its first migratory journey and subsequent breeding season.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at a relatively protracted age compared to other small passerines. Specifically, the time since birth at puberty is 78 days [tp = 78 days] when individuals are reared under the previously described thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This age at puberty is considerably longer than the 21 to 25 day interval sometimes reported in popular ornithological sources, likely because those figures conflate fledging with reproductive maturity. The onset of gonadal activity at this later date ensures that the young bird has completed its skeletal growth and built up sufficient fat reserves to support the energetic costs of egg production or territorial defense. In this species, first reproduction does not occur immediately upon reaching puberty; instead, individuals typically defer their first breeding attempt until the following calendar year, a strategy that allows for further refinement of foraging efficiency and social integration within the breeding colony.

The age at first successful reproduction in the Violet-green swallow is a key demographic parameter, and available data indicate that the time since birth at first brood is 365 days [tR = 365 days] in populations breeding under the characteristic thermal conditions of their active season, measured at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This interval corresponds to the typical delay between an individual's own hatching and the initiation of its first nesting attempt in the subsequent spring. Females produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], and within that single reproductive event, the typical fecundity is 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 eggs per clutch]. This modest annual reproductive output is balanced by a relatively high adult survival rate, a common life-history trade-off observed in aerial insectivores. The single-brooded strategy means that any nest failure within a given season represents a complete loss of that year's reproductive investment, placing a premium on nest site selection and parental vigilance.

Maximum recorded longevity in free-living populations of Tachycineta thalassina has been estimated from recapture data of banded individuals. The oldest documented birds reach a lifespan of approximately 9.1 years [am = approximately 9.1 years] under the standard active-season temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a remarkable duration for a bird of this small body size and high metabolic rate. This extended lifespan places the Violet-green swallow near the slow end of the life-history continuum for passerines of comparable mass, a pattern shared by other aerial insectivores that rely on ephemeral prey. The trade-off between high adult survival and low fecundity is likely shaped by the species' reliance on unpredictable insect resources, favoring a bet-hedging reproductive strategy. Comparative analyses with other North American swallows, such as the Tree swallow (Tachycineta bicolor), reveal that this longevity is among the highest recorded for any member of the genus, reflecting the benefits of a relatively stable montane breeding environment.
